idiom_name: tail-call step function with accumulator parameters; explicit loop where elimination is not guaranteed
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: make the recursive call the last action of the function, move all carried state into parameters (the accumulator), and let the base case be the only exit. Where the runtime guarantees or checks the elimination (proper tail calls, tailrec/@tailrec, musttail, become), leave the recursion in place and let the compiler emit the jump. Where it does not (JVM, CLR, CPython, Go, MRI, V8), the pattern's realization is the rewrite it describes: the parameters become mutable locals, the tail call becomes an assignment plus continue, and the base case becomes the loop guard - write that loop by hand instead of hoping the compiler removes the frames.
code_sketch:
loop with state s and input i:
    if terminal(s, i): return result(s, i)
    s, i = step(s, i)          # the tail call, executed as a jump
# where the runtime guarantees elimination, keep instead:
#     return f(step(s, i))
pitfalls: Assuming the transformation instead of checking it: in best-effort toolchains the same source grows the stack in debug builds or after an unrelated edit.
Mechanisms that only cover self-recursion (annotation-based elimination, most JITs) do not help mutual recursion; that needs a trampoline.
An eliminated tail call with a missing or unreachable base case loops forever, with no stack limit to stop it.

Wrong move: preferring tail recursion over body recursion for hot Erlang loops on any modern BEAM -> failure: since R12B body recursion uses similar memory and is often faster (it can return open-ended lists early and keeps arguments live for the garbage collector), so the 'optimization' costs speed and readability -> instead: write the clearer recursive form and measure; keep tail recursion where an unbounded loop or an explicit accumulator is what the algorithm is.

Wrong move: relying on an emitted .NET tail call in F# code that wraps the recursive call in try/finally or builds in Visual Studio Debug -> failure: those are documented blockers - the compiler falls back to a normal call (--tailcalls is off by default in Debug) and deep input overflows with no diagnostic -> instead: keep the loop outside the protected region, confirm the build's tail-call setting, and fall back to an explicit loop when the structure cannot preserve tail position.

Wrong move: assuming any trailing Lua call is optimized because it is syntactically last -> failure: only return f(x) outside to-be-closed scopes forms a proper tail call - a to-be-closed variable, a C-boundary frame, or any adjustment of the results silently keeps the frame, and the reused frame erases debug information about the caller -> instead: match the manual's exact tail-call criteria and expect flattened stack traces where the elimination fires.
